clue.text: Stylish earthenware drinking vessel

indicators.note: something drinking takes a liquid in, so the earthenware word swallows the vessel

parts.note: earthenware is made of fired clay
SS, steamship, is the usual abbreviation for a ship or vessel

explanation.surface: A fashionable clay drinking cup, the sort of thing sold in a craft shop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Earthenware drinking vessel' reads as one object, a mug, but 'drinking' is the container signal: the earthenware takes in the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something stylish has class and elegance, the colloquial adjective for which is this.

clue.text: Hourly you might hear this sound? Hardly!

definitions.text: Hourly you might hear this sound? Hardly!

parts.words: Hourly you might hear this sound? Hardly!
parts.note: a novelty clock bird calls out every hour, and its name is also slang for crazy, so the exclamation of disbelief fits the idea of madness

explanation.surface: Someone doubts that a sound really rings out on the hour.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird in a novelty clock pops out to call each hour; 'Hardly!' nods to the second sense, crazy or absurd.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic definition: the clock bird's call heard each hour, which is also slang for daft or mad.

clue.text: Place for poor little boy, timid creature keeping quiet

parts.note: Al is a short form of the boy's name Alan or Albert

indicators.note: one thing keeping another holds it inside, so the creature's letters enclose the quiet word

parts.note: a mouse is the proverbially timid animal
SH is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: A poor little boy and a frightened animal staying silent together.
explanation.walkthrough: 'keeping' is the container signal. An almshouse is a charitable home for the poor, historically run by a parish or guild.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a charitable dwelling built so that needy or elderly people can live there free.

clue.text: Aversion to industry opening hours

parts.note: a slot is a narrow opening

explanation.surface: A lazy worker objects to the factory's opening times.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Industry' means diligence here, not manufacturing, so 'Aversion to industry' is laziness.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: laziness, an unwillingness to work, is one of the seven deadly sins under this name.

clue.text: Pasture ploughed miles away from -estuary?

indicators.note: ploughed land is churned and turned over, so the word pasture is rearranged

explanation.surface: A field is turned by the plough some miles from the river mouth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ploughed' fits the farming picture but signals the rearrangement, giving UPSTREA.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: heading against the current takes you toward the river's source, away from where it meets the sea.

clue.text: Hollow stone mound one's left with to probable Christian burial site

parts.note: a pit is a hollow in the ground
a cairn is a heap of stones raised as a marker
one is I, and 's stands for is
and means together with

explanation.surface: A burial description: a hole and a stone heap left for someone presumably of the Christian faith.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Christian' is Fletcher Christian, leader of the Bounty mutiny, who settled on this Pacific island and probably died there.
explanation.definitionFit: Allusion: the mutineer Fletcher Christian is believed to have been buried on this remote Pacific island.

clue.text: Don't look to press when preparing newspaper article, say

definitions.text: Don't look to press when preparing newspaper article, say

parts.words: Don't look to press when preparing newspaper article, say
parts.note: a reporter drafting copy presses the keys without looking down at them, typing by feel

explanation.surface: Advice to a journalist about not glancing at the presses while writing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' seems to be the newspaper industry, but it is pressing keys.
explanation.definitionFit: Cryptic definition: the skill of using a keyboard by feel, eyes off the keys, as when writing copy.

clue.text: Have fare home, and places to sit — but no room for case

indicators.note: leaving no room for something drops it, so the outer letters are removed

parts.note: seating means places to sit
the case of a word is its outside, here its first and last letters S and G

explanation.surface: Dining at home, with chairs but no space for luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'but no room for' strips the case, the outer S and G, from SEATING.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to take one's meal in rather than going out or taking it away.

clue.text: Mass pretentious cardinal's done in Apostle style?

parts.note: arty means pretentiously artistic
cardinal is a deep red, the colour of a cardinal's robes

explanation.surface: A churchman hosts a showy Mass, and a cardinal is done in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cardinal' suggests a churchman but supplies the colour RED; most of the Apostles are said to have died for their faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: killed for one's faith, as tradition holds most of the Apostles were.

clue.text: Abroad, I'd no other alternative early opportunity

parts.note: abroad and afoot both mean in circulation, as a rumour is

indicators.note: an alternative is another version, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An exile laments having no other choice.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' seems to mean overseas but means going about, AFOOT; 'alternative' rearranges I'D NO OTHER into INTHEDOOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a first opening that gives a chance of further progress, like a salesman's wedged boot.

clue.text: I refuse to believe space traveller's clothing belonging to girl

indicators.note: clothing something wraps around it, so the traveller's letters go around the rest

parts.note: a comet travels through space; the 's is a link meaning is
of means belonging to
Fi is a short form of the girl's name Fiona

explanation.surface: An astronaut's suit turns out to belong to a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'space traveller' suggests an astronaut, and 'clothing' seems to be a spacesuit, but it is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: a colloquial retort of disbelief, telling someone to stop pretending.

clue.text: Unqualified leader dismissed by club

indicators.note: the leader is the first letter, and dismissing it removes it

parts.note: a putter is a golf club

explanation.surface: An unqualified captain is sacked by the club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'club' looks like a society but is a golf club, PUTTER, which loses its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: unqualified as in total or absolute, like an utter disaster.

clue.text: With blank scoreline, hard to sound excited

parts.note: a goalless draw is nil-nil, two noughts
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A goalless match is hardly a reason for fans to get excited.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamation: the noise people make when impressed or thrilled, functioning as a verb of sounding.

clue.text: Receiving unknown male, new honorary member of Drones Club, typically?

indicators.note: receiving takes something in, so the rearranged letters hold the rest
new signals a fresh arrangement of the word honorary

parts.note: Y is an algebraic unknown
he is a male pronoun

explanation.surface: A club welcomes an anonymous man as a new honorary member.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new' rearranges HONORARY into HOORANRY, which is 'Receiving' Y and HE. The Drones Club is P. G. Wodehouse's club for idle rich young men like Bertie Wooster.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: a loud upper-class young British man, the type Wodehouse's idle clubmen embody.

clue.text: Letter from Greek business graduate — one in the city

parts.note: mu is a letter of the Greek alphabet
an MBA is a Master of Business Administration
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A letter from a Greek MBA who works in the City of London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the city' seems to be London's financial district but is any city, here India's.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: India's largest city and financial capital, formerly called Bombay.

clue.text: Attend exclusively British and original exhibition of real ales

indicators.note: an original display presents the words real ales in a new, inventive order

explanation.surface: A beer festival with British real ales on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'original exhibition of' rearranges REAL ALES into EALLEARS after B.
explanation.definitionFit: Idiom: to listen with full attention, giving a speaker nothing but one's hearing.

clue.text: Voiced approval for Louis XIV, perhaps, and for King George I?

indicators.note: voiced means spoken aloud, so what follows is heard rather than read

parts.note: a French king's yes would be a royal oui

explanation.surface: Applause for two kings, one French and one English.
explanation.walkthrough: Oui is French for yes. A monarch says 'we' meaning 'I', so the answer stands in for King George's I.
explanation.definitionFit: Usage: the plural pronoun a sovereign uses in place of the singular when speaking of themselves.

clue.text: Series of moving beams comes down the way

parts.note: to light on something is to come down and settle on it
how means the way or manner

explanation.surface: A description of rays descending a path.
explanation.walkthrough: 'beams' could be timbers, but they are rays of light in a display.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a display of coloured lamps and lasers whose rays sweep and change.

clue.text: Musician raising collar with a beam

indicators.note: in a down answer, raising a word turns it upwards, reading it backwards

parts.note: to collar someone is to nab or arrest them
a joist is a supporting beam

explanation.surface: A musician lifts a collar using a beam.
explanation.walkthrough: 'collar' looks like a noun but is the verb, NAB, which 'raising' turns upside down to BAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: someone who plays a banjo is a kind of musician.

clue.text: Get old shoemaker's mould: one impervious to cracks?

parts.note: to age is to grow old
a last is the foot-shaped form on which a shoe is made

explanation.surface: A cobbler's mould grows old and cracked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cracks' looks like splits in old leather, but they are wisecracks; this rare word means someone who never laughs.
explanation.definitionFit: Rare word: a person who never laughs is unmoved by jokes, or cracks.

clue.text: Watch one learned to listen to, giving the time long ago

indicators.note: listening means the words are heard, so their sound matters, not spelling

parts.note: to watch is to eye, and a learned person is a sage

explanation.surface: Observing a wise old person, one hears of times past.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Watch' looks like a timepiece, fitting the time theme, but is the verb EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a prehistoric period when glaciers covered much of the earth.

clue.text: Briefly tolerated stifling parent guidance continually checking progress

indicators.note: stifling smothers something, so these letters close round the rating
briefly means cut short, losing the last letter

parts.note: stood means tolerated, as in stood for
PG is the film certificate for parental guidance

explanation.surface: A parent's advice was barely tolerated and smothered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' drops the last letter, giving STOO, and 'stifling' is the container signal. Stop-go was the British economic policy of alternately restraining and stimulating growth.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a pattern of alternately halting and resuming advance, as in economic policy.

clue.text: Steel band appearing in short sequence from Thames Pageant?

indicators.note: from places the pageant word before the sequence, as a clip taken from it

parts.note: the 2012 Thames River Pageant celebrated the Queen's Diamond Jubilee
a clip is a short excerpt from a film

explanation.surface: A steel band plays in a short film of the river pageant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Steel band' suggests Caribbean music but is a metal clamp for hoses.
explanation.definitionFit: Description: a metal strip tightened by a screw to secure a hose onto a pipe.

clue.text: Cry on discovering something axe split

parts.note: to bin something is to axe or discard it
to split is to leave, to go

explanation.surface: A shout when an axe splits something open.
explanation.walkthrough: 'split' looks like cleaving wood but means depart, GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamation: the shout of triumph when something is found or a game is won.

clue.text: Catchpole?

parts.note: the word joins catch, a freshwater fish one might land, and pole, an old measure of length; both senses fit one word

explanation.walkthrough: Catchpole looks like a surname or an old bailiff, but splits into catch (a fish) and pole (a measure of length).
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: a freshwater fish that anglers land, and an old measure of length also called a rod.

clue.text: Men ignoring teacher's expression of disapproval

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out, so these letters are taken away

parts.note: a tutor is a teacher; the 's is a link
OR, other ranks, means soldiers who are not officers, the men

explanation.surface: Soldiers paying no attention to their instructor, who clicks in disapproval.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ignoring' removes OR from TUTOR.
explanation.definitionFit: Exclamation: the clicking sound made with the tongue to show mild disapproval.

clue.text: Old territory turning over certain oil reserves

indicators.note: turning over flips the letters, reading them backwards
reserves means holds back, keeping the letters inside the phrase

explanation.surface: An old territory gives up certain oil reserves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reserves' looks like stocks of oil but holds AINOI inside 'certain oil'; 'turning over' reverses them to IONIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Historical: a region of ancient Greek settlement on the west coast of Asia Minor.

clue.text: Having no wish to get involved with rep

indicators.note: getting involved mixes things up, so the letters are combined and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone with no wish to get involved with a sales representative.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to get involved' mixes NO WISH and REP together.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: having something is possession, the state of owning it.

clue.text: Bags of time before alarm? Seconds

indicators.note: before places the time letter ahead of the alarm word

parts.note: a rouser is something that wakes you

explanation.surface: Lots of time before the alarm goes off? Only seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bags' as in 'bags of time' means plenty, but it is the old slang for loose trousers, Oxford bags.
explanation.definitionFit: Slang: wide loose trousers, as in Oxford bags, are known simply by this name.

clue.text: Rock band close to elegant fashion house

indicators.note: close to means the end, so the last letter is taken

parts.note: to hew is to shape or fashion

explanation.surface: A rock group playing near a stylish fashion house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fashion house' reads as a couturier but is two separate pieces, a verb and an abbreviation; 'close to' takes the last letter of 'elegant'.
explanation.definitionFit: Example: the English rock group of Pete Townshend and Roger Daltrey.
